newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia poll shows some friendships survive war.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia poll shows some friendships survive war.

text.p: Bosnia's first post-war polls allowing thousands of refugees to briefly return to their homes demonstrated hostility between former foes, but also that some could still be friends.

An estimated 20,000 Moslems, and around 4,000 Serbs, took advantage of the presence of the NATO-led peace force to vote on Saturday in regions from which they fled or were expelled during 43 months of vicious communal war.
For many, the scars of war were too deep to allow any thought of reconciliation.
For some, like Sarajevo Moslem Ferida Ribic, it was the loss of loved-ones in battle.

"If Serbs want to live with us again, ok. But I won't consort with them because they took away my boy," she said as she cast her ballot at the base of the Trebovic mountain where her son was killed in 1993.
Another Moslem voting in Bratunac, eastern Bosnia, broke into tears as he said: "It's very hard to look at these homes that were blurnt down. My two sons who were in Srebrenica are still missing."
Others, like Zaga Kenjac, a Serb refugee from Sarajevo now living in Serb-controlled east Bosnia, could not even imagine the possibility of the Moslem and Serb communities ever living together again.
"That's out of the question. I left two houses behind in Sarajevo."
Others still were pessimistic in the short term, but left open the possibility of some sort of reconciliation in the future.
"The only last solution is for us to stay apart, at least for some time to come," Zoran, a 26-year-old Serb plain-clothes policeman in Aliscici in northern Bosnia.

For a few, the depth of ethnic hatred knows no bounds. An elderly Serb refugee was heard telling a friend while watching Moslem refugees voting in Vlasenice in eastern Bosnia: "All (Moslems) should be exterminated for good. We didn't fight this bloody war so Moslems could vote in Bosnia."
But elsewhere across Bosnia, there were signs that old friendships had survived the recent blood-letting, and that at least some people were prepared to forgive and forget.
"We can live with the Serbs, we don't mind them and we never hated them," said Bahrudin Didic, a 45-year-old Moslem voting near Doboj in the north.
Fadil Pandur, a Moslem voting near his home town of Zvornik, east Bosnia, said he had greeted some of his old Serb frieds working at the polling station.
"They were pleased to see me and I was pleased to see them. We asked each other about our families and old acquaintances," he said.
In the polling booth, a crowd of Moslem refugees gathered around an elderly Serb who travelled to it to see his former neighbours for the first time in four years.

Outside another polling booth, villagers from two communities split by the war chatted by the roadside just like any neighbours parted for several years. One Serb man patted a Moslem woman on the back and said: "Please say hello to your husband."
Mira Zebic, a 41-year-old Moslem, said on returning to east Bosnia that she recognised all her husband's former colleagues, adding: "They all know me, I'm not scared."
Saying she was ready to live with Serbs again and bury the memories of bloodshed, she added: "We have to search for peace among people, in our souls and in our children."
